title: How many different Week 1 starting QBs has each NFL team used?
summary: Since the NFL expanded to 32 teams in 2002, no team has used more Week 1 starting quarterbacks than the Browns.
full_text:
Since the NFL expanded to 32 teams in 2002, no team has used more Week 1 starting quarterbacks than the Browns with 18. While the Browns aren't expected to add to that total this year with the announcement that  Deshaun Watson will start Week 1 , several teams are adding to their totals.

 Here's a look at how many different starting quarterbacks each team has utilized in Week 1 since 2002.

 Cleveland Browns - 18 
 Most Starts: Baker Mayfield (3) 
 Deshaun Watson will make his third opening-day start for the Browns in 2026, which will tie him with Baker Mayfield for the most by a Browns quarterback since the team returned to the NFL in 1999.

 Cleveland is 3-23-1 in openers since 1999. Watson has the chance to become the first Browns quarterback to win multiple openers in that time.

 Washington Commanders - 15 
 Most Starts: Jason Campbell (3), Robert Griffin III (3) and Kirk Cousins (3) 
 If Jayden Daniels makes his third straight opening-game start as expected, he'll match the most by a Washington quarterback since 2002. If he's able to continue the streak in 2027, he'll become the first Washington quarterback to start four straight since Mark Rypien from 1989 to 1993.

 Minnesota Vikings - 13 
 Most Starts: Kirk Cousins (6) 
 Kyler Murray has the most Week 1 starts for the Cardinals since 2002 and will now be the fourth different Week 1 starter in five seasons under coach Kevin O'Connell.

 

 Arizona Cardinals - 12 
 Most Starts: Kyler Murray (6) 
 Jacoby Brissett is expected to make his fourth opening-game start for his fourth different franchise (Browns, Colts, Patriots). That would be the most opening-game starts in the Super Bowl era without having multiple with any one team.

 Las Vegas Raiders - 12 
 Most Starts: Derek Carr (9) 
 The Raiders are adding a new starter to their total regardless of who gets the nod in Week 1, which will make it five straight years with a different Week 1 starter. It's either Kirk Cousins, who is 3-7 in his career on opening day, or Fernando Mendoza , who'd be making his NFL debut.

 New York Jets - 12 
 Most Starts: Mark Sanchez (4) and Chad Pennington (4) 
 Geno Smith is expected to make his third Week 1 start for the Jets, but his first since the 2014 season. No quarterback in the Super Bowl era has had a longer gap between opening-day starts for a single franchise. Currently the largest is by Brad Johnson, who started the 1998 and 2006 openers for the Vikings.

 Denver Broncos - 12 
 Most Starts: Peyton Manning (4) and Jake Plummer (4) 
 Since John Elway retired, no Broncos quarterback has started more than four season openers. Bo Nix is slated to start his third straight this season.

 Tampa Bay Buccaneers - 11 
 Most Starts: Josh Freeman (4) and Jameis Winston (4) 
 *Includes 2017, when Buccaneers started their season in Week 2 due to Hurricane Irma 
 Baker Mayfield is 3-0 with the Buccaneers in Week 1 after going 0-4 in such games with the Browns and Panthers. No Buccaneers quarterback has ever won four season openers.

 San Francisco 49ers - 11 
 Most Starts: Alex Smith (5) 
 Brock Purdy will be looking to improve to 4-0 in Week 1 games as the 49ers' starting quarterback. Maybe no surprise, but Steve Young (6-3) and Joe Montana (5-5) are the only Niners quarterbacks with more season-opening wins in the Super Bowl era.

 Chicago Bears - 10 
 Most Starts: Jay Cutler (8) 
 The first two Week 1 starts by Caleb Williams  came at home, but he'll make his first road start in an opener this season. The Bears are 4-15 in season openers on the road in the Super Bowl era.

 Houston Texans - 10 
 Most Starts: Matt Schaub (7) 
 C.J. Stroud will make his fourth opening-day start, trailing only Matt Schaub (7) and David Carr (5) for most in franchise history. Stroud is 1-2 in Week 1 games.

 Jacksonville Jaguars - 10 
 Most Starts: Trevor Lawrence (5) 
 Trevor Lawrence is expected to make his sixth straight opening-day start for the Jaguars. That would tie Mark Brunell for the longest streak in franchise history.

 Indianapolis Colts - 10 
 Most Starts: Peyton Manning (9) 
 Since Andrew Luck's retirement ahead of the 2017 season, the Colts are tied for the most season-opening starting quarterbacks with the Commanders (8 each). Daniel Jones is projected to make his second straight opening day start for the Colts.

 Miami Dolphins - 10 
 Most Starts: Ryan Tannehill (6) 
 *Includes 2017, when Dolphins started their season in Week 2 due to Hurricane Irma 
 Malik Willis is entering his fifth NFL season but will be making his first Week 1 start. He'll be the 11th opening-day starting quarterback for the Dolphins since Dan Marino retired.

 Pittsburgh Steelers - 9 
 Most Starts: Ben Roethlisberger (15) 
 Aaron Rodgers could be making his 19th and final opening-day start. That would tie Drew Brees for second most in the Super Bowl era and put him one shy of Tom Brady (20).

 Carolina Panthers - 9 
 Most Starts: Cam Newton (8) 
 Bryce Young is making his fourth opening-day start for the Panthers, but he's still searching for his first Week 1 win. The last quarterback to lose his first four opening-day starts? Baker Mayfield.

 Tennessee Titans - 9 
 Most Starts: Marcus Mariota (5) 
 The Titans have lost five straight season openers, the longest active streak in the NFL and the longest streak in franchise history. Cam Ward , the 2025 No. 1 pick, is slated to make his second straight opening-day start for Tennessee.

 Buffalo Bills - 9 
 Most Starts: Josh Allen (7) 
 Josh Allen has the most opening day starts for the Bills since 2002, but he still has some work to do to catch the Bills' franchise leaders. Joe Ferguson (12) and Jim Kelly (11) each have more.

 Los Angeles Rams - 8 
 Most Starts: Marc Bulger (6) 
 Reigning MVP Matthew Stafford  is slated to make his 18th opening-game start, which would tie him with Brett Favre for fourth most in the Super Bowl era.

 Stafford will also tie Marc Bulger for the most opening-day starts by a Rams quarterback since 2002.

 Atlanta Falcons - 8 
 Most Starts: Matt Ryan (14) 
 Tua Tagovailoa would be the sixth different Week 1 starting quarterback for the Falcons in the past six years if he gets the nod. If it's Michael Penix Jr ., he'd be the first repeat Week 1 starter for Atlanta since Matt Ryan started 14 straight openers (2008-21).

 Philadelphia Eagles - 7 
 Most Starts: Donovan McNabb (8) 
 Jalen Hurts is 5-0 in season-opening starts. The last quarterback to win his first six season openers? Roger Staubach, who went 9-0 in his career in opening games.

 New England Patriots - 6 
 Most Starts: Tom Brady (17) 
 The Patriots are only 2-4 in season openers since Tom Brady left for Tampa, including a loss in 2025 under Drake Maye .

 Kansas City Chiefs - 6 
 Most Starts: Patrick Mahomes (8) 
 Patrick Mahomes started his career 5-0 in season openers but is 1-2 in his past three, including a loss last season to the Chargers.

 His next Week 1 start will break a tie with Len Dawson for most by a Chiefs quarterback in the Super Bowl era.

 Cincinnati Bengals - 5 
 Most Starts: Andy Dalton (9) 
 Carson Palmer (7), Andy Dalton (9) and Joe Burrow (7) are the only Week 1 starters for the Bengals since 2004. Burrow is 2-4 in season openers and 3-9 in the first two games of the season.

 Seattle Seahawks - 5 
 Most Starts: Russell Wilson (10) 
 The reigning Super Bowl champions are 21-5 in Week 1 games this century but are just 2-2 in their past four.

 Sam Darnold is 3-3 in his career in six opening-game starts.

 Detroit Lions - 5 
 Most Starts: Matthew Stafford (12) 
 Jared Goff will be making his sixth straight opening game start, picking up where Matthew Stafford left off (12 straight). The last time the Lions had player who wasn't  the No. 1 pick of a draft start in Week 1 was Jon Kitna in 2008.

 Dallas Cowboys - 5 
 Most Starts: Dak Prescott (10) 
 Dak Prescott is expected to make his 11th season-opening start for the Cowboys. He'd be one shy of matching Troy Aikman (12) for the most…

title: How to bet the 2026 NFL season: Three bets to make on each team
summary: Will your NFL team beat its projected win total? What props should you target? Tyler Fulghum offers his three favorite bets for each team.
full_text:
The NFL season offers an almost unlimited amount of betting opportunities, from seasonlong win totals to individual player props and everything in between. It can be daunting.

 Don't worry. I've got you covered.

 Here are three wagers for each of the 32 franchises. Some picks look at the big picture, such as Super Bowl futures or division odds. Others zoom in on specific players, highlighting yardage totals, touchdown props or award chances. And for those who like long shots, we have a few of those too.

 Whether you're a futures-focused bettor mapping out the entire season or someone who prefers to target specific markets, this guide gives you a broad menu of options for every team. Consider it your all-in-one starting point for betting the 2026 NFL season.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change .

 Jump to: ARI  | ATL  | BAL  | BUF  | CAR  | CHI 
 CIN  |  CLE  | DAL  | DEN  | DET  | GB  | HOU 
 IND  |  JAX  | KC  | LAC  | LAR  | LV  | MIA 
 MIN  |  NE  | NO  | NYG  | NYJ  | PHI  | PIT 
 SEA  |  SF  | TB  | TEN  | WAS 

 

 

   Arizona Cardinals 
 •  UNDER 4.5 wins (-186)  
•  Trey McBride  receiving yards UNDER 999.5 (-110) 
•  Jeremiyah Love rushing TDs UNDER 5.5 (+100) 

 The Cardinals have the hardest schedule in the league this year, and I expect their record to reflect that. If Arizona struggles to stay competitive, McBride's receiving prop becomes difficult to clear because of statistical regression and a likely lack of consistent quarterback play. The under on Love adds another attractive fade of touchdown production. The rookie running back already suffered an ankle injury in training camp.

 

 
   Atlanta Falcons 

 • UNDER 6.5 wins (+130) 
• Fewest regular-season wins (15-1) 
• Bijan Robinson rushing TDs UNDER 8.5 (+100) 

 

 Atlanta could struggle to find consistency because of questions at quarterback and a suspect defense. Under 6.5 wins is the primary value play, while a bet on the fewest regular-season wins provides significant upside if the Falcons completely bottom out. The Robinson play complements the team unders by fading Atlanta's ability to consistently finish drives. Robinson can still post strong yardage numbers while falling short of this touchdown threshold.

 

 
   Baltimore Ravens 
 •  UNDER 11.5 wins (-140) 
•  Zay Flowers receiving TDs UNDER 5.5 (-120) 
•  Trey Hendrickson sacks UNDER 12.25 (-125) 

 The under on wins doesn't require a disastrous season, it simply requires the Ravens to fall short of an extremely high bar. Flowers' under on receiving touchdowns fits that thesis. He has been a productive receiver but has never scored more than five receiving TDs in a season, as his size limits his chances in the red zone. The Hendrickson under is another bet against elite individual production for a really good player. That's just a massive number to clear, even if he does stay healthy the entire season.

 

 
   Buffalo Bills 

 •  OVER 10.5 wins (-120) 
•  Win AFC East (-136) 
•  James Cook III rushing yards UNDER 1,224.5 (-110) 

 Buffalo is lined as the co-AFC favorite with Baltimore, and I agree that the team is going to be very good this season. I'm comfortable with the pricing on over 10.5 wins and an AFC East title. Those bets are closely correlated. If the Bills reach 11 or more victories, they're in excellent position to take back the division from the Patriots. The under on Cook's rushing yards is a bet against a massive number. Buffalo should have an elite rushing attack, but missing even one or two games makes this a difficult threshold to clear.

 

 
   Carolina Panthers 
 •  OVER 6.5 wins (-166) 
• OVER 2.5 division wins (-165) 
• Bryce Young passing TDs UNDER 20.5 (-110) 

 After last season's playoff appearance, Carolina feels poised to take a meaningful step forward. Over 6.5 wins is the anchor wager, while over 2.5 division wins suggests Carolina can capitalize on a mediocre NFC South and a solid home-field advantage. The under on Young's passing touchdowns can coexist with both bets if the Panthers lean on their running game and defense, which I fully expect Dave Canales to do, following the script from a season ago.

 

 
   Chicago Bears 

 • OVER 9.5 wins (+105) 
• Highest-scoring team in NFL (+900) 
•  Caleb Williams 30+ TD passes (+275) 

 Chicago's three bets are built around an offense that coach Ben Johnson has openly said he wants to break scoring records this year. The price betting the over on wins provides value on a team that could make a significant leap, while a bet on highest-scoring team in the NFL offers a much bigger payoff if Johnson's proclamations prove prophetic. Williams throwing 30-plus touchdown passes directly correlates with that outcome. If Williams takes a jump alongside Luther Burden III , Rome Odunze and Colston Loveland , watch out.

 

 
   Cincinnati Bengals 
 •  OVER 9.5 wins (-160) 
•  Win AFC North (+184) 
• Zac Taylor to win Coach of the Year (28-1) 

 

 Cincinnati feels like a sleeper team in the AFC. The bets on wins and the AFC North depend on the Bengals remaining healthy on offense, while Taylor winning Coach of the Year at these odds provides substantial upside if the revamped defense helps the Bengals become a more complete contender in the conference. The additions of DT Dexter Lawrence II , DT Jonathan Allen and DE Boye Mafe should pay immediate dividends on that side of the ball.

 

 
   Cleveland Browns 
 

 • UNDER 5.5 wins (+115) 
•  Fewest regular-season wins (+1050) 
•  Deshaun Watson passing yards UNDER 1,749.5 (-120) 

 Cleveland's portfolio of wagers is a straightforward assessment that this team is bad . The under bet on wins provides value if the Browns struggle to find stability, while a play on the fewest regular-season wins offers significant leverage on a true collapse. The under on Watson's passing yards prop fits particularly well because the number can be threatened simply by injury and/or ineffectiveness. Stocked up with bonus draft capital for 2027 and beyond, the Browns are actually incentivized to quietly tank this season.

 

 
   Dallas Cowboys 

 •  OVER 9.5 wins (+100) 
•  Division finishing position: 1 (+235) 
• Earn No. 1 seed in NFC (+1550) 

 On paper, Dallas looks like a legit contender entering this season. Bets on wins and winning the division are particularly attractive. We know the offense should be capable, but the upgraded personnel on the defensive side of the ball has me really intrigued with the ceiling of this team. That's why I'm willing to sprinkle a little on Dallas earning the NFC's No. 1 seed. That requires everything to break right, but the price is super attractive given the talent on this roster.

 

 
   Denver Broncos 
 •  OVER 9.5 wins (-110) 
•  AFC champions (+1025) 
• Jonah Coleman to win OROY (55-1) 

 After hosting the AFC Championship Game without its starting QB last season, Denver feels a little undervalued in the market. Over on wins is the core position, reflecting confidence that the Broncos can remain among the AFC's better teams. Bo Nix is back and healthy to start the season, and Denver should once again have an elite defensive unit, so the number to win the AFC feels mispriced. Coleman winning Offensive Rookie of the Year is the lottery ticket. It requires a major breakout, but Coleman has looked incredible in the preseason, with coach Sean Payton raving about his play.

title: Preseason NFL Power Rankings 2026: How all 32 teams stack up
summary: How do all 32 NFL teams stack up with under 10 days to go until the regular season? Plus, we picked out statistical milestones on the horizon for each team.
full_text:
With all 32 NFL teams making their final cuts Sunday night, it's the perfect time to size up the league in our Power Rankings just days away from the 2026 season .

 To form the list, our power panel of more than a dozen NFL analysts evaluates how all 32 teams stack up against one another, ranking them from No. 1 to 32.

 In addition to our 1-32 ranking, NFL Nation reporters picked a milestone to watch for each franchise this season. From 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan becoming the longest-tenured coach in 49ers history to Ravens running back Derrick Henry moving up to No. 6 on the career rushing list, there's plenty at stake beyond who wins  Super Bowl LXI . Let's dive into the record books, starting with two NFC West teams.

 Previous rankings: Post-Super Bowl , Postdraft 

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI |  ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 

 1. Los Angeles Rams 
 Postdraft ranking: 2 

 Milestone to watch: Quarterback Matthew Stafford  surpassing Philip Rivers for the sixth-most touchdown passes in NFL history during the regular season.

 Stafford has quickly climbed several career lists in recent years, including becoming the 10th quarterback to hit the 60,000 passing yards  milestone in Week 1 of 2025. He could check off another box with three more touchdown passes, eclipsing Rivers' career mark of 425. Given that Stafford averaged 2.7 touchdown passes per game in 2025, he could reach the milestone as early as Week 1 or Week 2 . Brett Favre is fifth on the list with 508 touchdowns. -- Sarah Barshop 

 

 
 

 2. Seattle Seahawks 
 Postdraft ranking: 1 

 Milestone to watch: Jaxon Smith-Njigba becoming the fourth player with at least 100 receptions in three of his first four seasons.

 Smith-Njigba had 100 receptions in 2024 before setting a franchise record with 119 last season on his way to winning AP Offensive Player of the Year . So his catch count will be worth watching come December. Brandon Marshall, Amon-Ra St. Brown and Michael Thomas are the only three players who've accomplished the feat -- though Rams star receiver Puka Nacua can also join the list in 2026. -- Brady Henderson 

 

 
 

 

 3. Buffalo Bills 
 Postdraft ranking: 4 

 Milestone to watch: Josh Allen  surpassing  Patrick Mahomes  for the most combined passing and rushing yards by a quarterback in his first nine NFL seasons.

 This would take Allen close to the end of the season, but it is well within reach. Allen is 3,782 yards away from eclipsing Mahomes (38,604), and Allen has not missed a start since his rookie season. He averages 590.1 rushing yards and 3,762.8 passing yards per season, so he could pass Mahomes with multiple games to spare. Breaking records is a common occurrence for Allen, and with new No. 1 receiver in DJ Moore added to the mix, he's primed to set many marks yet again. -- Alaina Getzenberg 

 

 
 

 4. Denver Broncos 
 Postdraft ranking: 3 

 Milestone to watch: Sean Payton moving into top 10 for career coaching wins.

 Payton, now in his fourth season with the Broncos, could move into the top 10 if the team plays at even a wild-card level. The Broncos, who were tied for a league-best 14 wins last season, would move Payton from the No. 13 spot (184) to No. 9 with at least nine wins. Currently, Hall of Famer Chuck Noll and Mike Tomlin are tied at No. 9 with 193. Marty Schottenheimer is No. 8 with 200 wins. -- Jeff Legwold 

 

 
 

 5. Philadelphia Eagles 
 Postdraft ranking: 5 

 Milestone to watch: Jalen Hurts becoming the third quarterback with at least 75 career rushing touchdowns.

 Hurts has 63 rushing TDs. He would join Allen (79) and Cam Newton (75) as the only signal-callers to reach 75. Last season, he had a career low since becoming the full-time starter in rushing attempts (105), yards (421) and touchdowns (eight). But he looked faster this summer when breaking from the pocket or executing designed runs. -- Tim McManus 

 

 
 

 6. New England Patriots 
 Postdraft ranking: 6 

 Milestone to watch: Wide receiver A.J. Brown totaling 1,000 receiving yards for the seventh season of his career.

 Brown has had four straight 1,000-yard seasons and has hit 1,000 in six of his seven NFL seasons. He could become one of seven WRs to have seven or more 1,000-yard seasons in his first eight years in the league, joining Mike Evans (eight), Lance Alworth (seven), Torry Holt (seven), Brandon Marshall (seven), Jerry Rice (seven) and Randy Moss (seven). -- Mike Reiss 

 

 
 

 7. Green Bay Packers 
 Postdraft ranking: 7 

 Milestone to watch: Edge rusher Micah Parsons becoming the first player to record at least 12 sacks in each of his first six NFL seasons since the metric became official in 1982.

title: 2026 NFL roster cuts: Biggest moves, more for all 32 teams
summary: Sunday was the deadline for NFL teams to finalize their 53-man rosters ahead of the 2026 season. We have full lists of cuts and big moves for all 32.
full_text:
We're less than two weeks from the start of the 2026 NFL season , when the Seahawks and Patriots meet in a Super Bowl rematch Sept. 9 . And with the preseason play wrapped up, front offices and coaching staffs have been busy around the league getting the rosters ready.

 The deadline for each team to finalize its 53-man roster was Sunday at 6 p.m. ET. Teams can still make moves, of course, before the opener, but getting down to 53 players by the deadline meant a lot of cuts and trades. Of note, the Cowboys released second-year running back Jaydon Blue , while the Colts retained quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr .

 Our NFL Nation reporters have the official releases and other moves for all 32 teams as news trickles out. Plus, they broke down the biggest moves to know.

General manager Brandon Beane stressed the importance of nailing down the position after the draft and having depth. The team also moved on from seventh-round cornerback  Toriano Pride Jr ., and Walker will likely be on the practice squad if he is not claimed. title: How active NFL players continue to redefine all-time sack list
summary: Myles Garrett's torrid pace up the all-time sack list paces seven active players making their moves among the greats.
full_text:
Last season, defensive end Myles Garrett won his second Defensive Player of the Year award after setting the NFL's single-season record with 23 sacks with the Cleveland Browns . 
 
 This season, he'll continue his climb up the NFL's all-time sack list as a member of the Los Angeles Rams  after a blockbuster trade  in June -- making the Rams favorites to win the Super Bowl, according to DraftKings Sportsbook. 
 
 Garrett enters the season with 125.5 career sacks, which is tied for 20th in NFL history and third among the other six active players --  Von Miller  (No. 9), Cameron Jordan  (No. 17), Calais Campbell  (No. 25), T.J. Watt  (No. 26), Danielle Hunter  (tied for No. 27) and Khalil Mack  (T-29th) -- in the top 30.  
 
 Joining the top 30 soon could be  Aaron Donald , who un-retired Sunday to join Garrett on the Rams' defensive line. Donald's 111 sacks currently sit two behind behind Mack and Sean Jones.  
 
 As for Garrett, he enters his 10th season in the NFL averaging approximately 14 sacks per season. If he were to replicate that production, he would tie Pro Football Hall of Famer Jason Taylor, who currently sits at No. 7 all-time. If Garrett were to have another historic season, he would surpass Michael Strahan (No. 6) and approach top-five all-time territory. 
 
 
 
 Miller, who recently signed with the  Dallas Cowboys  a couple of weeks ago, can also pass Strahan in his 15th season -- as he sits only three sacks behind him.   
 
 But Garrett's 125.5 career sacks are 10.5 more than any other player since his rookie season in 2017, according to ESPN Research. The pass rusher has recorded at least 14 sacks in each of the past five seasons, the longest such streak by any player since 1982. 
 
 If Garrett has 18.5 or more sacks this season, he will hold the record for the most over a two-season span since 1982, according to ESPN Research, and his current ascension up the all-time list ranks as the second-fastest pace among the top five all time behind only Reggie White.  
 
As we look at how the sack list is redefined this season, we'll highlight milestones across the NFL landscape 
 We will update this file each week as the active players move up, and we'll add nuggets and milestones throughout the season.

title: NFL stars who unretired: Aaron Donald joins Deion Sanders
summary: From Randall Cunningham to Bronko Nagurski to Jason Witten, here are the top players who came back for more.
full_text:
Defensive lineman Aaron Donald has followed through on his interest in returning to the NFL, agreeing to a one-year, $20 million deal with the Los Angeles Rams after two years in retirement. The decision thrust Donald, 35, into a select group of NFL players who interrupted retirement to get back on the field.

 How have others fared in similar situations? The list is relatively small, especially when you eliminate those whose "retirements" lasted less than one offseason. (Ahem, Brett Favre in 2008 and Tom Brady in 2022.) We also didn't consider players such as Michael Vick or Plaxico Burress , who returned to the field after time in jail.

 Here are 10 of the most notable efforts to return from retirement, ranked more or less in order of their success:

 

 

 1.  Randall Cunningham , QB 
 Cunningham had the best season of his career after retiring (for the first time). His career appeared over in 1995 when, at age 32, he received almost no interest on the free agent market. So Cunningham retired, moved home to Las Vegas and operated a granite and marble shop. But  Minnesota Vikings  coach Dennis Green convinced him to resume his career as a backup in 1997.

 When starter Brad Johnson was injured in 1998, Cunningham took over and led the team to an overall record of 15-1 (13-1 in Cunningham's starts) with an MVP-caliber season, throwing for 3,704 yards and 34 touchdowns. He earned a contract extension worth up to $28 million but was benched after six starts in 1999. He finished his career as a backup for the Ravens in 2001.

 
 

 2.  Deion Sanders , CB 
 Sanders fashioned an improbable second career as a part-time defensive back with the  Baltimore Ravens  after three full seasons away from the game. He initially called it quits following the 2000 season; he was so eager to get away that he forfeited part of an $8 million signing bonus he had received from Washington. In 2004, he signed with the Ravens and took No. 37 to match his age.

 In 25 games, including six starts, he intercepted five passes -- returning one for a touchdown -- and defended a total of 10 passes. But the Ravens missed the playoffs in both seasons and he retired for good in 2006.

 
 

 3.  Ricky Williams , RB 
 Williams played longer after his first retirement than he did before it, but he never replicated his early-career production. After rushing for a combined 4,470 yards from 2001 to 2003 for the  New Orleans Saints  and  Miami Dolphins , he retired rather than endure a 2004 drug suspension.

 At age 27, Williams moved to India to study yoga and holistic medicine. He returned to Miami for 12 games in 2005, rushing for 743 yards and six touchdowns but was suspended and moved to the CFL in 2006. A torn pectoral muscle limited him to one game for the Dolphins in 2007. Incredibly, he went on to play four 16-game seasons between 2008 and 2011. He managed only one 1,000-yard season among them before retiring permanently at age 34 after playing for the Ravens in 2011.

 
 

 4. Bronko Nagurski, RB/DT 
 

 Simply put, Nagurski was one of the baddest men ever to play pro football. In 1943, at age 35 and after five years away from a game that battered his body, Nagurski came out of retirement to help the  Chicago Bears  during World War II. Although he was best known as a running back, Nagurski was 6-foot-2 and 235 pounds and also played defensive tackle during an era of two-way players.

 Bears owner George Halas needed his help on defense more than anything, but he sneaked Nagurski onto the field for offense a few times, too. Nagurski played in eight games, rushing for 84 yards, and he had a touchdown in the NFL championship game. The Bears won the title with a 41-21 victory over Washington.

 
 

 5. Rob Gronkowski , TE 
 Toward the end of the 2018 season, Gronkowski spoke about the physical toll the game had taken on his body and said: "Try to imagine getting hit all the time and trying to be where you want to be every day in life. It's tough." But the Patriots, and the entire NFL world, were still surprised when he decided to retire in March 2019 at the age of 29.

 He sat out the 2019 season, but Brady recruited him back to the field after the quarterback's own brief retirement from the Patriots before they both joined the Buccaneers. Gronkowski helped the team win Super Bowl LV, catching two touchdowns to put Tampa Bay ahead 14-3 in the second quarter. He went on to play one more season before retiring for good at 33. In 28 regular-season games over two seasons with the Buccaneers, he caught 100 passes for 1,425 yards and 13 touchdowns.

 

 

 6. Eric Weddle 
 Weddle had been retired for two years when the Los Angeles Rams fell into crisis. With the 2021 playoffs looming, they lost starting safety Jordan Fuller to an ankle injury. Another safety, Taylor Rapp , was in the concussion protocol. Weddle had last played in 2019, and the Rams convinced him to return for their playoff run. He wound up playing in all four of their postseason games, starting two, and produced a legendary story. Weddle tore a pectoral muscle in the first half of Super Bowl LVI but continued playing en route to a five-tackle performance, as the Rams beat the Bengals 23-20. It was the one and only Super Bowl appearance of his 14-season career.

 

 

 7.  Marshawn Lynch , RB 
 Lynch retired three times before it stuck. His first attempt came in February 2016, when he famously tweeted an image of his cleats hanging from a power line. At age 29, relatively ancient for most running backs, Lynch had missed nine games for the Seattle Seahawks  in 2015 and by all appearances seemed ready to move on from the field. As it turned out, however, Lynch had one more goal to reach: playing for his hometown team in Oakland.

 After making his desires known in April 2017, Lynch convinced the Seahawks to trade his rights to the Raiders. In 21 games over the 2017-18 seasons, Lynch rushed for 1,267 yards and 10 touchdowns. He retired for a second time after that season, only to unretire again in December 2019 to rejoin an injury-ravaged Seahawks team. He played in one regular-season game, and two in the playoffs, collecting four touchdowns on 30 carries.

 
 

 8. Philip Rivers , QB 
 We include Rivers without a hint of recency bias. His story remains incredible. Rivers played 17 seasons for the Chargers, starting 240 games over that period, before retiring in 2020 at age 39. He moved into coaching at the high school level, and that's what he was doing when the Indianapolis Colts hit a crisis last season after losing quarterback Daniel Jones to a torn Achilles.

 With his team clinging to playoff hopes at 8-5, coach Shane Steichen convinced Rivers -- then 44 -- to help rescue the Colts' season. Rivers quite literally came out firing, jumping immediately into the starting lineup and getting rid of the ball at an average of 2.39 seconds per pass -- the second-fastest rate in a season for his career. He more than held his own in three starts, throwing for 544 yards and four touchdowns, but his time ended after the Colts were eliminated from playoff contention.

 Along the way, Rivers had gone 1,800 days between starts, the third most for a quarterback who did not play in between since at least 1950. He was also the fifth quarterback in NFL history to start a game at age 44 or older. (Another shows up later on this list!)

 
 

 9. Jason Witten 
 Witten retired late in the 2018 offseason, at the age of 35, after ESPN offered him the analyst's job for "Monday Night Football". He acknowledged some rough patches during his debut on television, and ultimately returned to the Cowboys after one season. There was little doubt that he could pull it off from a physical standpoint.

 He had earned Pro Bowl honors in 11 of his first 15 seasons and set a Cowboys record by playing in 235 consecutive games. Witten caught 63 passes while starting all 16 games in what turned out to be his final season with the Cowboys, before finishing his…

title: Bears DT Jordan van den Berg makes Gervon Dexter expendable
summary: Van den Berg, a sixth-round rookie, has been a surprise of training camp.
full_text:
LAKE FOREST, Ill. -- A moment after disengaging from his block,  Jordan van den Berg  saw  Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Sean Clifford escape the pocket. As if flipping a switch from brute strength to athleticism, the  Chicago Bears ' rookie defensive tackle accelerated towards the sideline and went airborne as he closed in on the quarterback.

 This late-third-quarter play from the Bears' second preseason game was one of several when van den Berg loudly announced his presence. The sixth-rounder was one of the surprise storylines of training camp and impressed Bears coaches enough to earn a spot on the 53-man roster.

 "He's a beast. He's an incredible athlete," coach Ben Johnson said. "He's still learning the game of football to a degree, and yet it's amazing what he brings to the table."

 The Bears made that official on Sunday morning when they shipped defensive tackle Gervon Dexter Sr . to the Atlanta Falcons for cornerback  Clark Phillips III  and a 2027 fifth-round pick. Van den Berg's emergence and role in the pass rush rotation is why Johnson recently dubbed the interior of the defensive line the most underrated on the roster.

 "When you start off with the [third-stringers] and then all of a sudden you show up and you catch our attention, then we've got to find ways to get you some reps with the twos, and if you continue to catch our attention, then we've got to find some ways to get you some reps with the ones because that's really how you evaluate what you have in the player," defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said.

 The last pick of the Bears' 2026 draft class may be its most consequential. Chicago chose to keep van den Berg over Dexter, the former second-round pick who started 33 games from 2023-25 and amassed 115 tackles, 13.5 sacks, 42 quarterback hits and 10 tackles for loss.

 Van den Berg was the last piece brought in to beef up the interior of the D-line after Chicago signed Neville Gallimore , Kentavius Street and James Lynch in free agency.

 

 Without an invite to the NFL combine, van den Berg had one opportunity to show off his talent to scouts at Gerogia Tech's pro day where he recorded 35 reps of 225 pounds on the bench press and ran a 4.9 second 40-yard dash. That would have been the sixth-fastest time by a defensive tackle at the combine, directly ahead of the 5.04 second 40-yard dash clocked by Florida defensive tackle Caleb Banks , who was drafted by the Vikings in the first round.

 Van den Berg's high ceiling and athletic testing drew the Bears to package two seventh-round picks to move up to No. 213 to draft him. Van den Berg scored the highest possible Relative Athletic Score (10.00), which measures an NFL draft prospect's athletic testing compared to others at their position over history. Van den Berg ranked second out of 2,278 defensive tackles from 1987 to 2026.

 That athleticism isn't surprising considering his pedigree. Van den Berg's grandfather, Francoise van den Berg, was a bodybuilder who was a two-time finalist at Mr. Universe competitions in the mid 1960s, where he finished runner-up to Arnold Schwarzenegger in 1967. His grandmother, Joan Ricci, set multiple South African national swimming records.

 The South African native moved with his family to the United States at 10 years old and was introduced to American football via "Invincible," the 2006 movie based on a true story about Philadelphia bartender Vince Papale earning a roster spot with the Eagles.

 After transitioning from playing rugby to football as a sophomore in high school, van den Berg started out as a wide receiver before moving from middle linebacker to defensive end to settling in at defensive tackle.

 Described as "a DNA match" by Bears national scout Brendan Rehoror for what Chicago coaches want from the defensive tackle position, van den Berg has proven he has the tools to help improve a struggling pass rush and the temperament required to win in the trenches.

 "I play with violence," van den Berg said. "This is a place where you're able to play with violence and get praise for it. I really enjoy that aspect of the game."

title: Early returns from Dexter Lawrence are promising for Bengals
summary: Over the last month of training camp, Lawrence has validated all of the excitement that accompanied his arrival into town.
full_text:
CINCINNATI -- First came the text. Then came the dance.

 Cincinnati Bengals defensive line coach Jerry Montgomery was at home with his family when his phone pinged with the news -- after weeks of subtle pursuit, the team had successfully traded for Dexter Lawrence II , one of the best defensive tackles in the NFL. Havana, Montgomery's 8-year-old daughter, hit a solid version of the "Sexy Dexy," Lawrence's sack celebration.

 Over the last month of training camp, Lawrence has validated all of the excitement that accompanied his arrival into town.

 "If he's not making the play, it's probably because there's four hands on him," Montgomery told ESPN. "If there's four hands on him, there's people running free. So now you have other guys making plays and then building confidence as a defense."

 And even when opponents have gotten ahold of Lawrence, the imposing lineman has found a way to get his 10.5-inch hands on players. Just ask Bengals running back Chase Brown .

 In one of the most memorable plays of training camp, Brown was trying to wriggle through the offensive line on a rushing play.

 Then Lawrence intervened. His hand emerged from the mass of bodies in the middle of the line of scrimmage and grabbed Brown by the shoulder. That was it for the play -- and Brown's shoulder pads, which needed repair.

 "It's stitched with what I'm assuming is a really strong thread, and he ripped the pad off," Brown said. "It's like I got grabbed by a monster or something. I couldn't get off."

 

 That seems to be a common theme among the locker room. When trying to describe Lawrence, teammates try to come up with an appropriate description that goes beyond the 6-foot-5, 350-pound characteristics listed in Cincinnati's media guide.

 Fellow running back Samaje Perine had another way to put it -- a brick wall.

 "There are big people all around the league," Perine said, "but usually when they're that big, they have a little give because they're a little bit fluffy-ish. But with him, it's just like a massive ball of muscle and there's no moving him."

 And throughout Cincinnati's training camp, the combination of Lawrence's unique physicality combined with someone enjoying a new environment has yielded a very potent player. Lawrence made his way to Cincinnati following a trade request submitted to the New York Giants , where he spent the first seven years of his career.

 Last year was statistically his worst. He finished with a career-low 0.5 sacks and his lowest pressure rate (5.3%) since 2020.

 In the lead-up to his first season with the Bengals, Lawrence has been adamant about not feeling the need to prove anything to anyone. The former first-round pick just wants to do what he has always done.

 "It's more about proving myself right," Lawrence told ESPN in July. "I know who I am."

 

 But Bengals center Ted Karras , who has had to block Lawrence almost every day for the past month, knew Cincinnati would be getting the best version of Lawrence following the trade.

 "You get an energy boost when you go to a new team," Karras said. "I think he's excited for a fresh start and he's been everything we could ever have imagined to anchor our defense."

 Karras said that Lawrence makes everyone around him "10 points better," which fits one of the big descriptions of the offense. Back at the NFL combine in late February, Cincinnati's coaches talked about adding "force multipliers" that elevate others on the team.

 That is exactly what Lawrence has done. And despite an already accomplished career and a lot of fanfare, he has been committed to doing what is asked of him by Montgomery and Cincinnati's staff.

 "You got guys like Dexter and  Jon Allen  who want to be coached," Montgomery said. "I've been around other guys that don't want to be coached. They think their s--- doesn't stink. (But) these guys want to be coached. They're pros. [They ask:] 'How can we get better?'"

 Montgomery doesn't want to make any early declarations on just how much better Cincinnati's defense will be with Lawrence in the middle. The Bengals spent the offseason adding pieces to improve a unit that finished 27th in points allowed per drive, per ESPN Research.

 But the early returns have been promising. In the joint practice against the Chicago Bears , Lawrence intercepted a ball he batted near the line of scrimmage. That created a turnover that sparked the defense to a big finish against the Bears, one of the NFC's most promising teams. 

 "He's a menace," Bears coach Ben Johnson said. "He's an issue. That's been the case for a number of years. I remember being in a joint practice setting a couple years ago, he wrecks practice. That's what he does."

 Over the last month, Lawrence has shown that if he's not creating problems in the middle, somebody else on the defensive line is. And there should be plenty of opportunities for him and others to show off their version of the "Sexy Dexy" as well.

summary: Houston knows it's on the right track but also knows it can't be complacent over last season's success.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- The standard for the Houston Texans ' defense under coach DeMeco Ryans is perfection.

 For example, let's rewind to Aug. 8, when lightning delayed a Saturday night practice, but once the weather calmed down, fans flooded the practice field to see a monsoon of domination from the Texans' defense.

 The defense brought sacks, intercepted quarterback C.J. Stroud twice and allowed minimal yardage throughout the evening. But it was a few positive offensive plays that frustrated defensive coordinator Matt Burke, calling his unit's performance "OK" despite ruling the day.

 

 "I wasn't happy with the way we started practice, to be honest with you," Burke said.

 How did Houston's defense start that evening? They allowed one rushing first down and a Stroud completion that was close to a first down. The rest of the practice turned into a highlight reel for the defense.

 "We're chasing perfection," Burke said. "I know no one gets there, but we're chasing it. We want to be better than we were last year."

 Ryans knows it's a process, but to "achieve the ultimate goal," they have to execute -- and passing last year's success isn't something they shy away from.

 Last season, the Texans finished 12-5, but their defense was No. 1 in yards allowed (277 per game), No. 2 in points allowed (17.4) and third in forced turnovers (29) while tormenting opposing quarterbacks.

 

 "It's a build to get there," Ryans said. "We're not afraid of the work that it takes to be put in to get there, and that's what we're achieving day by day."

 The unit stood the test last season, whether it was the Los Angeles Chargers ' Justin Herbert , Buffalo Bills ' Josh Allen , Kansas City Chiefs ' Patrick Mahomes or  Seattle Seahawks ' Sam Darnold , the Texans forced Pro Bowl signal-callers into a combined eight turnovers.

 The performance against Allen was on primetime and was the best one. It featured eight sacks (a career high for the Buffalo quarterback), and safety Calen Bullock  forced three turnovers (two interceptions and a forced fumble).

 Individual accolades poured in for the defense as a result.

 Cornerback Derek Stingley Jr ., defensive end Will Anderson Jr ., linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair , cornerback Kamari Lassiter  and Bullock were all named to the Pro Bowl. Defensive end Danielle Hunter was a second-team All-Pro selection, along with Stingley and Anderson earning first-team honors.

 But instead of focusing on their achievements, the Texans are working to improve in the areas where they fell short.

 "You never want to stay the same. Like if you stay the same, you're getting worse," Lassiter told ESPN. "Whenever you look back at last year, look at the plays that we made, and then you really look at the plays that we didn't make, it's like, 'How can I make those plays?' And once you look at it that way, there's so many ways you can get better."

 

 This offseason, they didn't make many changes to the defense, just minor adjustments.

 The biggest move was taking another swing at a Philadelphia Eagles safety following the failed acquisition of  C.J. Gardner-Johnson  (released after three games) last offseason by signing Reed Blankenship to a three-year $24 million contract. Houston also drafted Ohio State defensive tackle Kayden McDonald in the second round.

 So for the most part, the same stars and coaches will be leading the charge. 

 "It's just about the work we put in every day," Al-Shaair said. "You can't climb that mountain on Day 1, but you also can't look back either. It's just taking it one day at a time, one step at a time, and we're on the right track."

title: 2026 NFL offseason trade grades: Kaleb Johnson, Gervon Dexter
summary: We're making sense of eight big preseason deals, including Broderick Jones to the Cowboys.
full_text:
The main transaction window of the 2026 NFL offseason is over, with free agency and the draft long behind us. But teams are still leaning on trades to improve their rosters between now and Week 1. And we're grading the biggest swaps around the league, putting each deal into perspective for teams.

 The post-June 1 deals started with a bang. The Browns are  trading  edge rusher  Myles Garrett to the Rams for multiple draft picks -- including a 2027 first-rounder -- and edge rusher Jared Verse . The Patriots finally made their move to bring in Eagles wide receiver  A.J. Brown , giving up two draft picks. Did the Rams overpay in a massive return for Cleveland? Does Brown complete New England's offense? How do we feel about the Falcons acquiring offensive tackle Wanya Morris , the Texans getting wide receiver  Kayshon Boutte  and the Rams bringing back  wide receiver  Tutu Atwell ? And how did trades ahead of cut-down day impact the Cowboys, Steelers, Bears and Falcons?

 To determine each grade, we are looking at multiple factors, including on-field impact, salary cap implications, compensation, player value/age and the context of a team's short- and long-term outlooks. How large is the effect of this decision, and how sure are we that it's a good or bad choice? How does this affect a team's chance to win the Super Bowl, this season or in the future?

 Let's get into our grades, and check back throughout training camp and the preseason for more trade evaluations.

 
 See more: 
 Tracking trades over the summer 
 Grades from earlier in the offseason 

 
 

 

 Steelers trade RB Johnson to Packers 
 Packers get: RB Kaleb Johnson   
 Steelers get: 2028 sixth-round pick

 Packers grade: B 
 Steelers grade: B-

 Even before the news that Packers running back Josh Jacobs was placed on the commissioner's exempt list , which means he cannot practice or play, I liked this trade for the Packers. Johnson is the right sort of player to take a trade flier on. A wide zone running back at Iowa, Johnson was drafted early (pick 83) in the 2025 NFL draft relative to his skill set as a scheme-specific back, and he never found a great foothold in Pittsburgh as a rookie. Veteran Jaylen Warren stepped into  Najee Harris ' vacant role in the early-down rushing attack, and Kenny Gainwell emerged as a favorite passing down target of Aaron Rodgers .

 Stuck on special teams, Johnson made a critical error in a key moment of a Week 2 game. Down 17-14 in the fourth quarter to the eventual Super Bowl champion Seahawks, Johnson failed to field a live, bouncing kickoff ... then walked away from it as it rolled into the end zone and was recovered by the Seahawks for a special teams touchdown. This is the sort of rookie error that quickly put him in the doghouse -- Johnson only took 51 offensive snaps all season and took no more special teams snaps for the rest of the year.

 A fresh start might do Johnson well, and the Packers project as a team moving to more outside zone given the smaller, quicker players they're currently playing along the offensive line. In Jacobs' absence, Johnson can earn some early-down ball-carrying work in his preferred blocking style. Even if he's stuck behind MarShawn Lloyd to start the year, Lloyd's rough injury history creates even more opportunity for Johnson to see the field.

 The most likely outcome is still that Johnson is too limited of a player to be an impactful NFL back. But getting a former third-rounder for the cost of a future sixth, especially when the Steelers were clearly done with Johnson outright, is a good gamble.

 In that the Steelers are trading a 2025 third-round pick for a 2028 sixth-rounder, this isn't a win for the Steelers. The fact that they're getting anything for a player they were likely to cut is good work by GM Omar Khan. Even if Johnson ends up contributing for the Packers, the Steelers won't have much seller's remorse given their deep RB room. -- Solak 

 

 

 Bears trade DT Dexter to Falcons 
 Falcons get: DT  Gervon Dexter Sr . 
 Bears get: CB Clark Phillips III , fifth-round pick

 Falcons grade : A- 
 Bears grade : C

 This a good get for the Falcons, who needed defensive tackle help worse than perhaps any other team in the league. Free agent addition Da'Shawn Hand has missed most of training camp with a leg injury, leaving only bottom-of-the-roster contributors to fill the starting spot besides Brandon Dorlus . In Dexter, the Falcons grab a player big enough to play the nose next to Dorlus, but with enough power and pass-rush technique to still matter on passing downs. 

 Dexter had a pressure rate of 10.5% last season by NFL Next Gen Stat's charting, 11th among all defensive tackles and well above the league average for defensive tackles (7.4%). It is worth remarking that Dexter isn't really a penetrator who creates his own pressure -- he had only four quick pressures on the season, and his 1.13-second get-off was among the slowest of defensive tackles last season. Dexter is a pocket pusher who needs other pass rushers to create the first disruption. On a line that features Dorlus and second-year pro James Pearce Jr . (when he returns from his eight-game suspension ), that role can make sense.

 Dexter is on a contract year, which is one of the reasons he was available for a cheap return. If he has a good year in Atlanta, the Falcons might consider extending him... but they might also let him walk for a compensatory pick that replaces (or improves upon) the fifth-rounder they lost in letting him go.

 The Bears have waited on a leap forward in consistency from Dexter over the past two seasons, and absent a real breakout, have moved on to a rotation of veteran free agents ( Neville Gallimore , Kentavius Street and James Lynch ) and the exciting preseason play of rookie sixth-round pick Jordan van den Berg . All of those players, along with incumbent Grady Jarrett , are better suited to playing 3-tech than they are the nose. It's worth wondering if the Bears have a second incoming move to beef up their position at the nose.

 The Bears add CB Clark Phillips III , a depth player who has largely played outside in his career (727 snaps) but has the size to perhaps excel in the slot instead -- he has only 37 career snaps on the inside. The Bears anticipate playing fourth-round rookie Malik Muhammad in the slot as Kyler Gordon returns from injury, but depth at outside corner is also important given Jaylon Johnson 's injury background and Tyrique Stevenson 's history of uneven play. Phillips is nice for depth, but not much of a needle mover when a starter is going back the other way. -- Ben Solak 

 

 

 Steelers trade OT Jones to Cowboys 
 Cowboys get:  OT Broderick Jones , 2027 fourth-round pick 
 Steelers get: 2027 third- and sixth-round picks

 Cowboys grade: B- 
 Steelers grade: B

 This time last year, Broderick Jones was the starting left tackle for the Pittsburgh Steelers -- in line to replace the outgoing Dan Moore Jr . Hopes were high after Jones was drafted in 2023 out of Georgia, where he developed skills at right tackle in his last two seasons.

 But Jones struggled mightily when moved to left tackle with the Steelers. His pass block win rate on true pass sets last season was 65th of 68 qualifying tackles across the first 11 weeks of the 2025 season. A Week 12 neck injury then shelved Jones for the rest of the season . ESPN's Adam Schefter reported in April that Jones suffered setbacks during his recovery and his availability for offseason activities and Week 1 was uncertain. Those health concerns, along with his poor 2025 play, contributed to the Steelers' selection of Arizona State's Max Iheanachor in the first round of the 2026 draft. Jones did return to the field at the start of training camp, but the writing was on the wall for the lineman, who was still playing into the fourth quarter of Thursday's preseason game.

 The Steelers got a solid return for a player they could have feasibly cut on Sunday --…

title: Do NFL superteams usually win the Super Bowl? Will the Rams?
summary: The Rams are loaded this season, and basically everyone is picking them to win the Super Bowl. But preseason darlings of the past 35 years haven't always met expectations.
full_text:
Editor's note: This story originally published on Aug. 10 but has been re-published after news of  Aaron Donald 's return to the Rams . Los Angeles' Super Bowl odds have shifted from +550 to +500 over the past three weeks at DraftKings. 

 The 2026 Rams are the closest thing we've had to a preseason superteam in several years. Sean McVay's group was already a popular pick to win Super Bowl LXI before the offseason began. But then L.A. traded for Trent McDuffie and signed Jaylen Watson , shoring up the secondary at the expense of a potential Super Bowl opponent in the Chiefs. The move to draft Ty Simpson as Matthew Stafford 's successor struck a curious tone, but general manager Les Snead responded with the mother of all high-stakes moves, trading Jared Verse and three picks to the Browns for reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett .

 Unsurprisingly, the Rams have become prohibitive favorites to win the Super Bowl after their aggressive moves this offseason. Picking any other team to win the Lombardi Trophy at this point would almost require coming up with some sort of explanation for what happened to the Rams along the way.

 And yet, we have to look back only one year to remind ourselves how NFL seasons can play out entirely differently once players get on the field. In 2025, 68 ESPN personalities picked  their AFC and NFC champions, along with an eventual Super Bowl winner, before the season kicked off. Not a single person picked the Seahawks or Patriots. I predicted the  Chiefs and Packers , who combined for exactly zero playoff wins. Preseason darlings like the Chiefs, Lions and Commanders each missed the playoffs altogether.

 Was 2025 just a weird year? And how often do heavily favorited superteams such as the 2026 Rams actually win the Super Bowl? I decided to take a more comprehensive look through history to get a sense of how confident we can be that Los Angeles will be the last team standing come Feb. 14 .

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 To do so, I'm going to look at the 15 largest preseason favorites since 1990 and see how their seasons played out. I'll be using the preseason odds compiled at Pro Football Reference from 1990 to 2025 and compare them with the odds posted for this season's Super Bowl at  DraftKings . The Rams have odds of +550 at DraftKings to win the Super Bowl, while nobody else in the league is shorter than +1000. After we adjust for the vigorish and convert the betting lines into probabilities, the Rams have an implied 12.5% chance of winning this season's Super Bowl, putting them 5.1 percentage points ahead of the second-placed Bills and Ravens.

 While the absolute number might be a better sense of how the market views a particular team, I'm going to use the latter figure to sort through our top 15 teams (well, 16, if we're including the 2026 Rams). There were plenty of seasons in the 1990s where two or three superteams -- such as the 49ers and Cowboys -- were seen as significantly better than the rest of the competition. I want to get a sense of what it was like for the teams that truly separated from the pack before the season began, as appears to be the case for this Rams squad.

 Did those teams hold up to their preseason expectations? Was the market overconfident about their chances? Let's go team by team before using the lessons from those 15 earlier cases to talk about what it means for the 2026 Rams and their chances of winning McVay and Stafford their second title.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 2026 Rams | 2021 Chiefs | 2019 Patriots 
 2018 Patriots | 2017 Patriots | 2009 Patriots 
 2008 Patriots | 2007 Patriots | 2002 Rams 
 2001 Rams | 1998 Packers | 1997 Packers 
 1996 49ers | 1995 49ers | 1994 49ers | 1990 49ers 
 Can this season's Rams win the Super Bowl? 

 
 

 

 2017 New England Patriots 
 Implied odds: 19.8% 
 Gap to the rest of the NFL: 11.5% 
 Result: Lost Super Bowl LII to the Eagles, 41-33 

 I wouldn't have guessed that the 2017 Patriots stood out in terms of Super Bowl odds more than any other New England team from the Tom Brady-Bill Belichick era, but let's contextualize this. The Pats were coming off that legendary 34-28 win over the Falcons in Super Bowl LI . Brady was getting Rob Gronkowski back from injury after the star tight end missed the playoff run with a back ailment , while Belichick added a new star receiver to the mix in Brandin Cooks . After a 14-2 season and with Brady motivated by the four-game suspension he took for the Deflategate scandal, you could understand why the Patriots were heavy favorites to repeat as champs.

 

 Some things went as expected. Brady won the league MVP award. Cooks and Gronkowski each topped 1,000 yards. The Pats went 13-3 and took home the top seed in the AFC.

 Others did not. Belichick's team started 2-2 and needed a last-minute comeback win over a 4-12 Texans team to avoid opening the season 1-3. The Pats righted the ship quickly, but they were trailing by 10 points in the fourth quarter of the AFC title game and were down nearly three scores to the Jaguars, only for Myles Jack 's fumble recovery touchdown to be overturned. Two late touchdown passes to Danny Amendola controversially pushed the Pats into the Super Bowl.

 There, well, nothing went as planned. The Patriots defense had quietly been a mess all year, finishing the regular season ranked 31st in DVOA. The offense covered up the weakness by holding on to the ball and getting out to early leads. The Eagles were heavy underdogs with backup quarterback Nick Foles in for the injured Carson Wentz , and you know what happened next. Brady threw for 505 yards and three touchdowns, still the record for an NFL quarterback in a losing effort, but the defense couldn't stop Foles & Co. The Pats fell 41-33.

 

 
 

 2007 New England Patriots 
 Implied odds: 20.9% 
 Gap to the rest of the NFL:  10.5% 
 Result: Lost Super Bowl XLII to the Giants, 17-14 

 Are you sensing a trend? This was another Patriots team that rode offseason optimism about its offensive additions to high hopes before falling short in the Super Bowl. The 2006 Pats had blown a 21-3 lead to the Colts in the AFC Championship Game , but they also weren't far removed from winning three titles between 2001 and 2004. Brady had improved as a quarterback over that time, and during the offseason, Belichick had rebuilt the offense by trading for Randy Moss and Wes Welker and signing Donte' Stallworth.

 What happened next is one of the more notable seasons in NFL history. The Pats were caught spying on the Jets during a 38-14 blowout victory in Week 1, turning a team that had been the underdog favorites during their win over the Rams in 2001 into the villains of the NFL. On the field, the Patriots blew defenses away with their spread attack, as Brady produced arguably the greatest season in league history under center. The Patriots went 16-0 in the regular season, winning their average game by nearly 20 points.

 By the time the postseason came around, though, the cracks were beginning to show. Brady threw three picks in the AFC title game , but with Philip Rivers playing through a torn ACL and LaDainian Tomlinson limited by injury to three touches, the Chargers couldn't take advantage in a 21-12 defeat. And in the Super Bowl, again as heavy favorites, the Patriots were upset by a Giants team that was able to control Brady in the pocket with its pass rush.

 

 

 
 

 1996 San Francisco 49ers 
 Implied odds: 19.2% 
 Gap to the rest of the NFL:  9.6% 
 Result: Lost in divisional round to the Packers, 35-14 

 The 49ers were the preseason favorites to win the Super Bowl in 1994, 1995 and 1996. Their status as the third team on this list might have more to do with a lack of competition in the AFC than anything else. The Bills were among the Super Bowl favorites earlier in the decade, but after a 7-9 season in 1994 and a 10-6 campaign in 1995, they had fallen back to the pack. title: Are the Seahawks ready for Jadarian Price to lead run game?
summary: With Zach Charbonnet set to miss the first four weeks on the PUP list, Seattle will turn to its first-round pick.
full_text:
RENTON, Wash. -- Rookie Jadarian Price is ready to lead the Seattle Seahawks ' backfield while it waits for Zach Charbonnet to return. Or at least as ready as he can be.

 Except for the week he missed with a minor injury, Price has had a strong summer, displaying the vision, decisiveness and athleticism that made him the Seahawks' choice with the 32nd pick in April's draft. He has looked as good as advertised -- and in some ways better.

 But that all comes with the caveat that when Price steps onto Lumen Field for Seattle's Sept. 9 opener against the New England Patriots , the team's presumed RB1 will be making his NFL debut having not played a single snap in the preseason. Getting Price as prepared as possible for actual football has been trumped by the Seahawks' desire to preserve him for the long haul.

 "He's done a great job. He really has -- all three downs," coach Mike Macdonald said last week. "He's a rookie in terms of, there's going to be things that we're going to attack in his game that will show itself in games. We haven't been afforded the luxury of having the bodies right now at running back to give him the reps in a [preseason] game that we would normally give to a rookie runner."

 

 The best guess is that the Seahawks are planning, for now, to roll with Price as their lead back while mixing in a heavy dose of George Holani , whose receiving and pass-blocking skills seem perfectly suited for third-down work.

 Emanuel Wilson will be the power complement to those two, though the free agent addition is on the mend from an undisclosed injury that sidelined him for the last couple of weeks and kept him out of Seattle's preseason finale Friday against the Kansas City Chiefs . Wilson has been running off to the side with trainers during practice, suggesting he won't be out for long.

 Whatever plan Seattle has going into Week 1 will start to change once Charbonnet returns.

 Last year's co-starter appears to be in the closing stretch of his recovery from February surgery to repair an ACL tear he suffered in January. He's still on the physically unable to perform list, meaning he will miss the first four games of the season at a minimum.

 Whenever Charbonnet is all the way back, it's easy to envision the Seahawks splitting the work in their backfield fairly evenly between him and Price the way they did last season with Charbonnet and Kenneth Walker III .

 

 Price may not have the same fifth gear as Walker, but he looks like he can replicate at least some of the explosiveness Seattle's backfield lost when the Super Bowl LX MVP signed with Kansas City in free agency.

 "He's good, man," linebacker Ernest Jones IV  said early in camp. "Mature for his age, you can tell. You don't get too many words out of him, but he's working. He got me today, man. He had a hell of a route on me today. ... I think he's going to help us. He's doing everything right and he's got a great group of backs in front of him that's kind of teaching him the way."

 Jones was referring to how Price had beaten him for a touchdown during a 7-on-7 rep, getting open behind the 2025 second-team All-Pro before making an over-the-shoulder catch on a deep ball from Sam Darnold . Price's ability to contribute in the passing game was one of the biggest questions about his skill set after he finished his Notre Dame career with only 15 receptions over three seasons as a backup. But he's answering it.

 "He's a special player," Darnold said after the Seahawks' Aug. 21 joint practice in Nashville, Tennessee. "He's a really special player. He brings a different facet to the offense that only a guy like him can bring. Whether it's catching passes out of the backfield, catching screens, running in between the tackles, outside the tackles. He can really do it all, and I know he's just going to continue to get better and learn."

 Holani got much of the work with the No. 1 offense that day, with Price still ramping back up. The cautious, long-game approach the Seahawks have taken with their top pick could mean even more growing pains out of the gate than they'd usually expect from a rookie. But they seem willing to live with that for the trade-off of keeping him healthy.

 "He's shown that we're really confident in him going into Week 1," Macdonald said. "He's earned that decision for us to feel good about it. Even though in just about any other circumstance, you'd definitely want really any rookie to get preseason exposure and experience."
